lessons.title: What Rust Is
lessons.concept: A compiled language without a garbage collector
lessons.summary: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector. The compiler checks types, ownership and borrowing before your program runs, then produces a native program.
lessons.rule: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before the program runs, then produces a native executable.

lessons.title: Hello, Rust
lessons.concept: Functions and stdout
lessons.summary: A small Rust program gives you the whole development loop: write a function, let the compiler check it, run it, and inspect what appeared on stdout.
lessons.rule: Execution begins in `fn main()`. `println!` is a compile-time-checked macro that writes a formatted line to stdout when the program runs.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.concept: let, mut, and shadowing
lessons.summary: A binding names a value. Rust keeps that binding fixed by default, asks for `mut` when the value must change, and uses a fresh `let` when you want to shadow it.
lessons.rule: `mut` permits mutation; shadowing hides the old binding behind a new one.

lessons.title: Printing Values
lessons.concept: Format strings and placeholders
lessons.summary: A format string is a checked template: each placeholder has a value, and the finished line follows the template exactly, including spaces and alignment.
lessons.rule: Every formatting placeholder must have a value known to `println!`.

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.concept: Integer and floating-point types
lessons.summary: Choosing a number type records a promise about range and precision. Rust makes conversions explicit so that promise cannot change silently at an arithmetic boundary.
lessons.rule: Numeric conversions are explicit because ranges and precision differ.

lessons.title: Booleans
lessons.concept: Comparisons and logical operators
lessons.summary: A comparison produces a `bool`, and a branch requires one. `&&` and `||` can skip their right-hand expression as soon as the result is known.
lessons.rule: `if` requires `bool`; Rust has no implicit numeric truthiness.

lessons.title: Characters & Text
lessons.concept: char, &str, and Unicode
lessons.summary: Rust text has several useful units: bytes for encoding, Unicode scalar values for `char`, and sometimes multiple scalars for one visible symbol.
lessons.rule: `String` indexing by an arbitrary byte is forbidden because UTF-8 boundaries matter.

lessons.title: Reading rustc
lessons.concept: Expected, found, spans, and help
lessons.summary: A compiler diagnostic is a map back to the source: find its primary span, compare expected with found, and make one intentional fix before reading follow-up errors.
lessons.rule: Repair the first causal error before chasing its downstream messages.

lessons.title: Compound Types
lessons.concept: Tuples, arrays, and annotations
lessons.summary: Rust checks scalar and compound types before the program runs.
lessons.rule: A tuple mixes types by position; an array holds one type with a fixed length.

lessons.title: Operators & Casting
lessons.concept: Arithmetic, overflow, and as
lessons.summary: Numeric operations have type-dependent bounds. Choose checked, wrapping or saturating behavior explicitly and validate narrowing conversions.
lessons.rule: Numeric operands need compatible types; choose the overflow policy explicitly.

lessons.title: Block Expressions
lessons.concept: Statements, tail values, and semicolons
lessons.summary: A block can perform statements and then produce one final value.
lessons.rule: No semicolon means a tail value; a semicolon turns it into `()`.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.concept: Returns and expression bodies
lessons.summary: A function signature is a contract the compiler enforces at every call site.
lessons.rule: The last expression without a semicolon is the return value.

lessons.title: Parameters
lessons.concept: Typed inputs and arguments
lessons.summary: A function signature is a compact contract for every caller.
lessons.rule: Parameters need explicit types; arguments must satisfy them.

lessons.title: Control Flow
lessons.concept: if and match as expressions
lessons.summary: Expressions and loops model decisions without hidden coercion.
lessons.rule: `if` is an expression; every branch must produce the same type.

lessons.title: Ranges
lessons.concept: Exclusive and inclusive boundaries
lessons.summary: Range syntax makes boundaries visible instead of hiding an off-by-one rule.
lessons.rule: `a..b` excludes `b`; `a..=b` includes `b`.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.concept: for, while, loop, break, and continue
lessons.summary: Choose the loop form that states why repetition ends.
lessons.rule: Prefer `for` for iteration; use `loop` when `break` defines the exit.

lessons.title: Parsing Values
lessons.concept: Turning text into typed data
lessons.summary: Parsing crosses from untrusted text into a type with explicit success or failure.
lessons.rule: Parsing returns `Result` because input text is not guaranteed to fit the target type.

lessons.title: First References
lessons.concept: Borrowing for read-only access
lessons.summary: A shared reference lets a function read a value while the caller keeps ownership.
lessons.rule: `&T` borrows `T` for read-only use without transferring ownership.

lessons.title: Using Methods
lessons.concept: Dot syntax and chained transformations
lessons.summary: Method syntax puts an operation beside the value it acts on.
lessons.rule: Read a method's `self` parameter to learn its ownership effect.

lessons.title: Handling Failure
lessons.concept: Result without panic
lessons.summary: `Result` keeps expected failure in the function's type instead of turning it into a crash.
lessons.rule: Use `Result` for failure the caller can reasonably respond to.

lessons.title: Inspecting Values
lessons.concept: Debug, dbg!, and stderr

lessons.rule: `dbg!` returns its argument and writes diagnostic output to stderr.

lessons.rule: `match` is exhaustive: every variant must be handled.

lessons.rule: A blocking call occupies an executor worker without yielding, so unrelated tasks can stall.

lessons.title: Own Tasks with JoinSet
lessons.concept: Completion order, errors, and task lifetime
lessons.summary: Keep the tasks you start in a collection whose lifetime and results are explicit.
lessons.rule: Spawning starts an independent task; awaiting its result is a separate responsibility.

lessons.title: Bound Work Before Spawning
lessons.concept: Semaphore permits and bounded queues
lessons.summary: Put the limit before the expensive resource allocation, not after an unbounded queue has formed.
lessons.rule: A concurrency limit and a queue-size limit protect different resources.

lessons.title: A Graceful Shutdown Protocol
lessons.concept: Stop admission, signal, and wait
lessons.summary: Cancellation becomes reliable when the operation owns a protocol and a completion point.
lessons.rule: Requesting shutdown is not the same as observing that all workers have stopped.

lessons.title: macro_rules!
lessons.concept: Pattern-based code generation
lessons.summary: macro_rules! matches syntax patterns and expands to code.
lessons.rule: Macros work on tokens before type checking, which is why they can vary in arity.

lessons.title: Procedural Macros
lessons.concept: Derive, attribute, and function macros
lessons.summary: A procedural macro is a compiler plugin written in Rust.
lessons.rule: Proc macros execute at compile time, so they need a host-native build.

lessons.title: cfg & Features
lessons.concept: Compiling different code per target
lessons.summary: cfg decides which code is compiled at all.
lessons.rule: `#[cfg(...)]` excludes selected code before name and type checking, but source syntax still has to parse. Disabling default features on one dependency edge does not prohibit another edge from enabling them.

lessons.title: unsafe Rust
lessons.concept: Five powers and their invariants
lessons.summary: `unsafe` unlocks five operations; it does not turn off the borrow checker.
lessons.rule: `unsafe` is a claim about an invariant, not permission to skip the rules.

lessons.title: FFI
lessons.concept: extern "C", repr(C), and raw pointers
lessons.summary: FFI needs explicit ABI, layout, ownership and validity contracts; unsafe code must uphold the foreign function requirements.
lessons.rule: `repr(C)` follows C layout rules for the target; it is not a recursive layout, ownership or pointer-validity guarantee.

lessons.title: Performance
lessons.concept: Allocation, iterators, and measuring
lessons.summary: Rust is fast by default; the wins left are allocation and algorithm.
lessons.rule: Measure representative workloads with the target optimization profile; debug timings do not predict release performance.

lessons.title: Rust Idioms
lessons.concept: Newtype, builder, and typestate
lessons.summary: Rust's patterns push mistakes from runtime to compile time.
lessons.rule: A newtype costs nothing at runtime and buys a real compile-time guarantee.

lessons.title: Macro Hygiene
lessons.concept: Resolve generated names without accidental capture
lessons.summary: Resolve generated names without accidental capture.
lessons.rule: Rust macros track syntax context so identifiers introduced by a macro do not casually collide with names at the call site.

lessons.title: Token Trees
lessons.concept: Match Rust syntax as nested tokens, not raw text
lessons.summary: Match Rust syntax as nested tokens, not raw text.
lessons.rule: `macro_rules!` consumes token trees with balanced delimiters.

lessons.title: Proc-Macro Boundaries
lessons.concept: Separate host-time generation from target code
lessons.summary: Separate host-time generation from target code.
lessons.rule: A procedural macro is compiled for and runs on the build host, then emits tokens for the target crate.

lessons.title: Raw Pointers
lessons.concept: Represent an address without borrow guarantees
lessons.summary: Represent an address without borrow guarantees.
lessons.rule: Creating `*const T` or `*mut T` is safe; dereferencing one is `unsafe` because validity, alignment, initialization, and aliasing are now the programmer's proof obligations.

lessons.title: Representation & Layout
lessons.concept: Make a data layout contract explicit at a boundary
lessons.summary: Make a data layout contract explicit at a boundary.
lessons.rule: Rust's default layout may change for optimization and is not an FFI contract.

lessons.title: Unsafe Traits
lessons.concept: Make an implementation promise other unsafe code relies on
lessons.summary: Make an implementation promise other `unsafe` code relies on.
lessons.rule: An `unsafe` trait means incorrect implementation can cause undefined behavior in code that trusts it.

lessons.title: Benchmark & Profile
lessons.concept: Find the real bottleneck before optimizing
lessons.summary: Find the real bottleneck before optimizing.
lessons.rule: A benchmark measures a stable workload; a profiler explains where its time or allocations go.

lessons.title: WASM Is Not the Browser API
lessons.concept: Targets, host imports, and local execution
lessons.summary: A WebAssembly module runs with the imports its host supplies, not with every capability of the computer.
lessons.rule: Compilation target and host imports determine what a module can do.

lessons.title: Linear Memory Boundaries
lessons.concept: Checked offsets, lengths, and borrowed slices
lessons.summary: A guest pointer is an offset into guest memory, not a host pointer you can blindly dereference.
lessons.rule: Check offset plus length without overflow before making a borrowed view.

lessons.title: Budget a Local Runtime
lessons.concept: Independent CPU, memory, output, and storage limits
lessons.summary: Local execution still needs independent limits for the resources a guest can consume.
lessons.rule: A timeout does not replace memory, output, or filesystem quotas.

lessons.title: Explain Ownership
lessons.concept: Moves, Copy, Drop, and scope
lessons.summary: Explaining ownership well means naming the guarantee, not the syntax.
lessons.rule: Ownership tracks resource responsibility; move, borrow and clone express different contracts.

lessons.title: Why Borrowing Works
lessons.concept: Aliasing and mutation rules
lessons.summary: The borrowing answer is about aliasing versus mutation.
lessons.rule: Aliasing XOR mutation, checked over the region a borrow is used.

lessons.title: Lifetime Reasoning
lessons.concept: Relationships, not object duration
lessons.summary: Lifetimes are about relationships, and saying so is the answer.
lessons.rule: A lifetime constrains borrows; it never keeps anything alive.

lessons.title: Option vs Result
lessons.concept: Absence, failure, and propagation
lessons.summary: Pick the type that matches what the caller must decide.
lessons.rule: `Option`: absence is normal. `Result`: the caller needs the reason.

lessons.title: Send and Sync
lessons.concept: Thread-safety marker traits
lessons.summary: Two marker traits decide what may cross a thread boundary.
lessons.rule: T is `Sync` exactly when &T is `Send`.

lessons.title: Box, Rc, and Arc
lessons.concept: Ownership and allocation choices
lessons.summary: Three pointers, three different ownership questions.
lessons.rule: Pick by ownership count first, then by thread boundary.

lessons.title: dyn Trait vs Generics
lessons.concept: Dispatch and code size tradeoffs
lessons.summary: Generics preserve concrete types; trait objects provide a common interface with dynamic dispatch.
lessons.rule: Choose dispatch from API flexibility, ownership and measured performance; neither choice guarantees a smaller or faster program.

lessons.title: Reasoning About unsafe
lessons.concept: Sound abstractions and invariants
lessons.summary: `unsafe` is a claim about an invariant, not a disabled checker.
lessons.rule: `unsafe` moves the obligation to you; it never removes it.

lessons.title: Atomics and Ordering
lessons.concept: Relaxed, Acquire/Release, SeqCst
lessons.summary: An atomic is a value several threads may touch without a lock.
lessons.rule: Atomicity and ordering are separate promises; Relaxed gives only the first.

lessons.title: Deadlocks
lessons.concept: What the borrow checker does not prevent
lessons.summary: Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks.
lessons.rule: Data-race freedom is a compile-time guarantee; deadlock freedom is a design one.

lessons.title: Channels vs Mutex
lessons.concept: Moving ownership or sharing it
lessons.summary: Share memory by communicating, or communicate by sharing memory.
lessons.rule: Channels move ownership; a mutex shares it. Pick by data flow.

lessons.title: Async vs Threads
lessons.concept: Waiting versus computing
lessons.summary: Async makes waiting cheap and threads run work in parallel; neither owns all I/O or all CPU.
lessons.rule: Choose concurrency and parallelism from the workload; async tasks still execute on threads.

lessons.title: Blocking an Executor
lessons.concept: Why one sync call stalls a runtime
lessons.summary: One blocking call can stall an entire async runtime.
lessons.rule: Never block an executor thread: yield, or move the work off it.

lessons.title: Cancellation Safety
lessons.concept: Dropping a future mid-await
lessons.summary: In Rust, an async task is cancelled by dropping its future.
lessons.rule: Cancellation is a drop; state between awaits must survive it or not exist.

lessons.title: Stack and Heap
lessons.concept: Where values live and what a move copies
lessons.summary: Ownership and storage location are separate questions; draw the handle and the allocation.
lessons.rule: A move transfers ownership; handle placement and optimized instructions are not language guarantees.

lessons.title: Virtual Memory
lessons.concept: Pages, faults, and resident size
lessons.summary: Every pointer you see is virtual, and the kernel decides what it means.
lessons.rule: Virtual size, committed memory and residency are different measurements; inspect the actual platform.

lessons.title: Syscalls and Buffering
lessons.concept: Where the cost of IO actually is
lessons.summary: A syscall is a controlled trip into the kernel, and it is not free.
lessons.rule: Buffering can combine small writes; measure the boundary cost and handle errors explicitly.

lessons.title: TCP vs UDP
lessons.concept: Streams, datagrams, and trade-offs
lessons.summary: TCP gives you a reliable ordered stream; UDP gives you datagrams and nothing else.
lessons.rule: TCP: ordered, reliable, head-of-line blocked. UDP: messages, no promises.

lessons.title: HTTP/1.1, 2, and 3
lessons.concept: Head-of-line blocking per layer
lessons.summary: Each HTTP version fixed the blocking problem one layer lower.
lessons.rule: HTTP/2 shares TCP’s ordered byte delivery; QUIC separates delivery of different streams.

lessons.title: What TLS Guarantees
lessons.concept: Identity, confidentiality, integrity
lessons.summary: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, and identity — in that order of confusion.
lessons.rule: Encryption without verified identity stops eavesdroppers, not an active impostor.

lessons.title: Backpressure
lessons.concept: Bounded queues and load shedding
lessons.summary: A queue with no limit is a crash with a delay.
lessons.rule: Every queue needs a bound and a policy for what happens at that bound.

lessons.title: Transactions and Isolation
lessons.concept: Which anomaly each level allows
lessons.summary: Isolation is the letter in ACID people actually get wrong.
lessons.rule: Choose transaction boundaries and isolation for a named invariant on a named database.

lessons.title: Indexes and B-trees
lessons.concept: Composite index selectivity, planner choices, skip scans and write cost
lessons.summary: An index is a sorted structure that trades write cost for read speed.
lessons.rule: Leading columns often make a composite B-tree scan selective, but later-column predicates can still use an index, including through skip scan. The actual choice depends on the database, statistics and query plan.

lessons.title: CAP in Practice
lessons.concept: What happens during a partition
lessons.summary: CAP is about what happens during a partition, not a menu of three.
lessons.rule: Specify the consistency model and failure protocol; quorum arithmetic alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: Idempotency and Retries
lessons.concept: Making at-least-once safe
lessons.summary: A retry is only safe if the operation is idempotent.
lessons.rule: An idempotency key needs an enforced request/outcome contract, not just a header.

lessons.title: Caching and Invalidation
lessons.concept: Staleness budgets and stampedes
lessons.summary: Caching is easy; deciding when the cache is wrong is not.
lessons.rule: Every cache needs a bound, an eviction policy, and a stated staleness budget.

lessons.title: Complexity in Practice
lessons.concept: Constants, cache, and amortised cost
lessons.summary: Big-O tells you how something scales, not how fast it is.
lessons.rule: Complexity predicts growth; constants decide which one is faster today.

lessons.title: Hashing and Collisions
lessons.concept: Why Rust seeds its hasher
lessons.summary: A hash map is O(1) until an adversary picks your keys.
lessons.rule: Hash choice is a security decision whenever the keys are attacker-controlled.

lessons.title: Choosing a Test
lessons.concept: Unit, property, fuzz, integration
lessons.summary: Different bugs need different tests, and naming them is the answer.
lessons.rule: Choose tests for named failure modes and independent evidence; test labels alone prove little.

lessons.title: API Design and Semver
lessons.concept: Making misuse impossible to express
lessons.summary: A good API makes the wrong call impossible, not merely documented.
lessons.rule: Encode the invariant in the type; documentation is not enforcement.

lessons.title: Profiling First
lessons.concept: Measure, change one thing, measure
lessons.summary: Measure first: the bottleneck is almost never where it feels like it is.
lessons.rule: Profile, change one thing, measure again. Guessing is not optimising.

lessons.title: FFI and ABI
lessons.concept: Ownership across the C boundary
lessons.summary: FFI needs explicit ABI, layout, ownership and validity contracts; unsafe code must uphold the foreign function requirements.
lessons.rule: repr(C) fixes layout; ownership across the boundary is documentation you enforce.

lessons.title: Live Coding: Two Sum
lessons.concept: Clarify duplicates, indices, and complexity first
lessons.summary: Clarify duplicates, indices, and complexity first.
lessons.rule: State the contract before reaching for `HashMap`: may one index be reused, can values repeat, and what should happen when no pair exists? Then explain the O(n) time and O(n) space tradeoff.

lessons.title: Design an LRU Cache
lessons.concept: Combine lookup speed with recency updates
lessons.summary: Combine lookup speed with recency updates.
lessons.rule: Explain why a hash map alone cannot evict the least recent key in O(1).

lessons.title: Design a Parser
lessons.concept: Separate tokenization, grammar, and diagnostics
lessons.summary: Separate tokenization, grammar, and diagnostics.
lessons.rule: A strong answer defines input ownership, source spans, recovery strategy, and whether the parser returns a tree or events.

lessons.title: Debugging Out Loud
lessons.concept: Form a hypothesis and request one discriminating fact
lessons.summary: Form a hypothesis and request one discriminating fact.
lessons.rule: Do not edit randomly during an interview.

lessons.title: Communicate a Tradeoff
lessons.concept: Tie a choice to constraints and a failure mode
lessons.summary: Tie a choice to constraints and a failure mode.
lessons.rule: A senior answer does not call one tool universally best.

lessons.title: Clarify Requirements
lessons.concept: Turn a broad prompt into boundaries and invariants
lessons.summary: Turn a broad prompt into boundaries and invariants.
lessons.rule: Ask about scale, latency, durability, consistency, trust boundaries, and expected failure.

lessons.title: Review Rust Code
lessons.concept: Prioritize correctness, API contracts, then style
lessons.summary: Prioritize correctness, API contracts, then style.
lessons.rule: Start with soundness, data loss, and observable behavior before naming cosmetic issues.

lessons.title: Explain an Incident
lessons.concept: Describe conditions and controls, not one guilty person
lessons.summary: Describe conditions and controls, not one guilty person.
lessons.rule: A useful postmortem separates trigger, contributing conditions, detection gaps, impact, and durable actions.

lessons.title: Cell, RefCell and Runtime Borrows
lessons.concept: Interior mutability without confusing Send and Sync
lessons.summary: Interior mutability changes how access is checked; it does not remove the safety contract.
lessons.rule: Runtime borrow checking still enforces exclusivity; ownership transfer and concurrent sharing have different trait bounds.

lessons.title: Copy, Clone and Cow
lessons.concept: Implicit duplication, explicit cloning and lazy ownership
lessons.summary: Ask which bytes are shared, copied or allocated before choosing an ownership conversion.
lessons.rule: `Clone` semantics depend on the type; `Cow` delays ownership conversion until an operation needs it.

lessons.title: UTF-8 and Editor Offsets
lessons.concept: Bytes, Unicode scalars, graphemes and UTF-16 positions
lessons.summary: Text positions need a declared coordinate system before they can be exchanged or sliced.
lessons.rule: Validate the coordinate system, source revision and UTF-8 boundaries before slicing text.

lessons.title: Iterator Ownership and Laziness
lessons.concept: Borrowing iteration, consuming iteration and deliberate collection
lessons.summary: An iterator pipeline describes work; the item type and terminal operation determine ownership and execution.
lessons.rule: Trace the receiver, iterator item type and consumer before making a move or allocation claim.

lessons.title: Fn, FnMut and FnOnce
lessons.concept: Capture ownership and how a closure uses its environment
lessons.summary: The call trait follows what the closure does with captures, not just whether `move` appears.
lessons.rule: `move` controls capture ownership; the closure body determines its call-trait capabilities.

lessons.title: Pin, Unpin and Future Polling
lessons.concept: Stable pointees without confusing the pointer with its allocation
lessons.summary: `Pin` constrains moving a pointee through a pointer; moving that pointer can remain valid.
lessons.rule: `Pin` protects the pointee’s address-sensitive contract; `Unpin` governs safe access that can move it.

lessons.title: Send Across await
lessons.concept: Task state, 'static bounds and non-Send locals
lessons.summary: Inspect which values survive a suspension before deciding whether a future satisfies `Send`.
lessons.rule: `Send` is determined by the future’s actual retained state; `async move` does not upgrade non-`Send` types.

lessons.title: Lock Scope Across await
lessons.concept: Synchronous blocking, suspension and cancellation-safe critical sections
lessons.summary: Keep synchronous critical sections short and make suspension while holding a guard an explicit design decision.
lessons.rule: Waiting for a lock, holding a lock during suspension and doing CPU work are separate concerns.

lessons.title: Async Traits and dyn Compatibility
lessons.concept: Native async methods, returned futures and explicit type erasure
lessons.summary: Native async trait methods and dynamic dispatch are separate interface choices.
lessons.rule: Check dyn compatibility, future lifetime and `Send` bounds independently.

lessons.title: Error Types at API Boundaries
lessons.concept: Absence, invalid input and contextual failure
lessons.summary: An error type should preserve the distinctions the caller needs to handle.
lessons.rule: Choose error structure from caller decisions; absence, failure and defaulting are different policies.

lessons.title: Orphan Rules and Newtypes
lessons.concept: Implementing foreign traits without conflicting implementations
lessons.summary: A local wrapper creates a distinct type whose behaviour your crate can own.
lessons.rule: A newtype creates a distinct local type; an alias only gives an existing type another name.

lessons.title: Integer Boundaries and Conversion
lessons.concept: Checked arithmetic and deliberate narrowing policies
lessons.summary: Input bounds and arithmetic policy are part of the algorithm’s contract.
lessons.rule: Choose the numeric domain and overflow policy explicitly, and widen before the operation when that is the proof.

lessons.title: What Rust Is, from C
lessons.concept: Native code and the same machine, with checks before it runs
lessons.summary: Rust compiles to native code like C, with no garbage collector and no virtual machine; what changes is that rustc proves memory safety for safe code before the program runs.
lessons.rule: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before the program runs, then produces a native executable.

lessons.title: What Safe Rust Rules Out
lessons.concept: Undefined behaviour excluded, bugs still possible
lessons.summary: Safe Rust rules out the memory and thread bugs that are undefined behaviour in C, but not leaks, deadlocks, panics or wrong logic.
lessons.rule: Safe Rust has no undefined behaviour: use after free, double free, dangling references, out-of-bounds access, null dereference, uninitialised reads and data races are rejected or checked; leaks, deadlocks, panics, logic errors and wrapping arithmetic in release builds are not.

lessons.title: Reading rustc Diagnostics
lessons.concept: Compile-time errors instead of run-time crashes
lessons.summary: Where a C program compiles and crashes later, rustc stops with an error code, the exact spans involved and a suggested fix; reading them in order is a skill worth learning first.
lessons.rule: Repair the first causal error before chasing its downstream messages: read its code and primary span, then the labels, notes and help, fix the cause and recompile.

lessons.title: From printf to println!
lessons.concept: Format strings checked at compile time
lessons.summary: `println!` checks its format string against its arguments while compiling; `printf` trusts you until run time.
lessons.rule: `println!` is a macro: placeholders and arguments are matched during compilation, so a missing or mistyped argument is a compile error, not undefined behaviour.

lessons.title: const by Default
lessons.concept: Immutable bindings, mut and shadowing
lessons.summary: In Rust a binding is immutable unless you write `mut`, and a new `let` can reuse a name for a new value or even a new type.
lessons.rule: `let` bindings are immutable by default; `mut` opts in to mutation, and shadowing with a new `let` creates a new binding instead of changing the old one.

lessons.title: Integer Overflow and Casts
lessons.concept: Defined overflow policy and explicit conversions
lessons.summary: Rust never converts between integer types silently, and overflow is always defined: a panic in debug builds, wrapping in release builds, or exactly the policy you call.
lessons.rule: Integer types never mix implicitly; choose the overflow policy (`checked_`, `wrapping_`, `saturating_`) and the conversion (`From`, `TryFrom`, `as`) explicitly.

lessons.title: Functions Are Expressions
lessons.concept: Tail values replace return and the ternary
lessons.summary: A Rust block evaluates to its last expression, so functions return without `return`, and `if` replaces the ternary operator.
lessons.rule: A block's value is its final expression without a semicolon; adding the semicolon turns it into a statement, and the block evaluates to `()`.

lessons.title: From for(;;) to Ranges
lessons.concept: Ranges, iterators and loop with a value
lessons.summary: `for` iterates over ranges and collections, `..=` includes the end safely, and `loop` can hand a value out with `break`.
lessons.rule: `for` iterates over a range or collection; `a..b` excludes `b`, `a..=b` includes it, and `loop` with `break value` replaces sentinel variables.

lessons.title: From malloc/free to Ownership
lessons.concept: One owner frees, exactly once
lessons.summary: Every heap value in Rust has exactly one owner; passing it by value moves ownership, and the end of the owner's scope frees it exactly once.
lessons.rule: One value has one owner; a move transfers ownership and ends the old binding, and the remaining owners drop in reverse declaration order at the end of their scope.

lessons.title: Pointers to References
lessons.concept: Shared or exclusive, checked at compile time
lessons.summary: A reference is a pointer the compiler checks: shared `&T` for reading, or one exclusive `&mut T` for writing, never both at once.
lessons.rule: At any point a value has either any number of shared borrows `&T` or exactly one mutable borrow `&mut T`, never both; a borrow lends access without transferring ownership.

lessons.title: Pointer + Length to Slices
lessons.concept: A view that carries its own bounds
lessons.summary: A slice `&[T]` is a pointer and a length in one value, so functions receive their bounds and every index is checked.
lessons.rule: A slice borrows a contiguous range of another value's elements; it allocates nothing, and indexing past its length panics instead of reading out of bounds.

lessons.title: Dangling Pointers and Lifetimes
lessons.concept: The compiler checks what the comment promised
lessons.summary: A lifetime names how long a reference is valid, so the compiler rejects the dangling pointer that a C comment could only warn about.
lessons.rule: A lifetime annotation relates the output borrow to the input borrows; it never extends how long any value lives.

lessons.title: Struct Copies: Copy and Clone
lessons.concept: Bitwise copies only for plain data
lessons.summary: Rust copies a struct implicitly only when it is plain data marked `Copy`; anything that owns a resource moves, and a deep copy is an explicit `.clone()`.
lessons.rule: `Copy` permits implicit bitwise duplication for types that own no resources; `Clone` is an explicit duplication whose cost depends on the type.

lessons.title: Structs and Methods
lessons.concept: The receiver states the pointer contract
lessons.summary: Methods live in an `impl` block, and the receiver (`&self`, `&mut self` or `self`) states what C expressed with `const` pointers and comments.
lessons.rule: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies, and `self` consumes the value; read a method's receiver to learn its ownership effect.

lessons.title: Tagged Unions to Enums
lessons.concept: A tag that cannot disagree with its payload
lessons.summary: A Rust `enum` is a tagged union whose tag and payload cannot disagree, and `match` must handle every variant.
lessons.rule: `match` must be exhaustive: every variant has to be handled, and an arm with a guard does not count as covering its pattern.

lessons.title: NULL and errno to Option and Result
lessons.concept: Absence and failure in the return type
lessons.summary: Absence is `Option<T>` and failure is `Result<T, E>`, both in the return type, so a caller cannot use the value without handling the other case.
lessons.rule: Return `Option<T>` when a value may simply be absent and `Result<T, E>` when the caller needs to know why an operation failed.

lessons.title: char Arrays to Strings
lessons.concept: Owned UTF-8 with a length, not a NUL
lessons.summary: A Rust `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer with a stored length and no NUL, and text is never indexed by a single integer position.
lessons.rule: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes and `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values; indexing a string by an integer is forbidden because a byte offset may fall inside a character.

lessons.title: Headers and make to Cargo
lessons.concept: Modules, pub and the crate as the build unit
lessons.summary: Cargo replaces headers and Makefiles: the crate is the unit of compilation, modules are found from `mod` declarations, and items are private until marked `pub`.
lessons.rule: Items are private to their module unless marked `pub`; `src/main.rs` is the default binary target and `src/lib.rs` the library target.

lessons.title: unsafe, Raw Pointers and FFI
lessons.concept: Where Rust hands the proof back to you
lessons.summary: Raw pointers, `unsafe` and `extern "C"` let Rust do what C does, and `unsafe` marks exactly where you take over the proof that the compiler cannot do.
lessons.rule: Creating a raw pointer is safe; dereferencing it needs `unsafe`, which is a claim that the pointer is valid, aligned, initialised and correctly aliased, not a switch that turns the checks off.

lessons.title: pthreads to std::thread
lessons.concept: Locks that own data, threads that own their captures
lessons.summary: Rust threads are the same OS threads as pthreads, but a `Mutex` owns the data it protects and the compiler rejects data races.
lessons.rule: `thread::spawn` needs a `Send + 'static` closure, so captures are moved in; shared state goes in `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, and the lock guard unlocks when it drops.

lessons.title: Node.js runtime vs compiled Rust
lessons.concept: Ahead-of-time compilation to a native executable
lessons.summary: Rust is compiled ahead of time to a native executable: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before anything runs, and there is no garbage collector or built-in event loop.
lessons.rule: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before the program runs, then produces a native executable.

lessons.title: Garbage collection vs deterministic drop
lessons.concept: Deterministic drop at the end of scope
lessons.summary: V8's garbage collector frees objects whenever it decides; Rust drops each value at the end of its owner's scope, in an order you can read from the code.
lessons.rule: At scope end, remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order; struct fields drop in declaration order.

lessons.title: TypeScript types vs Rust types
lessons.concept: Types the compiler enforces, and its diagnostics
lessons.summary: TypeScript types are erased and can be bypassed with `any` or `as`; Rust types are enforced by rustc, which builds nothing until its diagnostics are fixed.
lessons.rule: rustc refuses to build a program with a type error: read each diagnostic's code, span and labels, and repair the first causal error before chasing its downstream messages.

lessons.title: console.log vs println!
lessons.concept: Compile-time checked formatting
lessons.summary: `println!` replaces `console.log`, and rustc checks every placeholder against its arguments before the program runs.
lessons.rule: Execution starts in `fn main()`; `println!` and `format!` are macros whose placeholders are checked during compilation.

lessons.title: const and let vs let and let mut
lessons.concept: Immutable bindings, mut and shadowing
lessons.summary: Rust's plain `let` is stricter than `const`: without `mut` you can neither reassign the binding nor change the value through it.
lessons.rule: `let` is immutable, `let mut` permits change, and a new `let` with the same name shadows the old binding.

lessons.title: Number vs Rust integer types
lessons.concept: Explicit numeric types and overflow
lessons.summary: Every JavaScript `Number` is an f64. Rust makes you pick a numeric type, convert between types explicitly and decide what happens on overflow.
lessons.rule: Numeric types never mix implicitly: convert with `From` or `try_from`, and choose checked, wrapping or saturating arithmetic where overflow is possible.

lessons.title: JavaScript functions vs fn
lessons.concept: Typed parameters and tail expressions
lessons.summary: A Rust function declares every parameter type and returns its final expression; there are no default parameters and no implicit coercions.
lessons.rule: Every parameter has a type, arguments must match it exactly, and a block's final expression without a semicolon is its value.

lessons.title: Truthiness vs bool, if and match
lessons.concept: No truthiness: conditions are bool
lessons.summary: Rust has no truthy or falsy values: a condition must be a `bool`, and `if` and `match` are expressions whose branches share one type.
lessons.rule: `if` requires a `bool`, and every branch of an `if` or `match` expression must produce the same type.

lessons.title: Classes and objects vs structs
lessons.concept: Data in structs, behaviour in impl blocks
lessons.summary: A class becomes a `struct` for the data and an `impl` block for the methods, and each method's receiver says whether it reads, changes or consumes the value.
lessons.rule: `&self` reads, `&mut self` modifies and `self` consumes: the receiver tells the caller what a method does to the value.

lessons.title: TypeScript unions vs enums
lessons.concept: Discriminated unions as enums
lessons.summary: A TypeScript discriminated union becomes a Rust `enum` whose variants carry their own data, and `match` must handle every variant.
lessons.rule: An enum variant carries its own data, and `match` must cover every variant; a guard narrows an arm but never excuses a missing case.

lessons.title: null, undefined and ?? vs Option
lessons.concept: Absence as Option<T>
lessons.summary: `null` and `undefined` become `Option<T>`: absence is part of the type, and `?.` and `??` become `and_then`, `map` and `unwrap_or`.
lessons.rule: Use `Option<T>` when a value may be absent and `Result<T, E>` when the caller needs the reason; `unwrap_or` replaces `??`, not `||`.

lessons.title: Array methods vs iterators
lessons.concept: Lazy iterator pipelines
lessons.summary: `map` and `filter` on an array run at once and build new arrays; Rust's iterator adapters do nothing until a consumer such as `sum`, `find` or `collect` pulls values.
lessons.rule: Iterator adapters are lazy: a consumer such as `sum`, `find`, `collect` or a `for` loop drives the work, one item at a time.

lessons.title: Objects and Map vs HashMap
lessons.concept: Keyed data with HashMap and entry
lessons.summary: Plain objects used as dictionaries become `HashMap<K, V>`: typed keys, no prototype keys, and `entry` for update-or-insert in one lookup.
lessons.rule: `entry(key).or_insert(default)` looks the key up once and returns a mutable reference to the value, whether or not it was already there.

lessons.title: UTF-16 strings vs UTF-8 String
lessons.concept: UTF-8 bytes, chars and lengths
lessons.summary: JavaScript strings count UTF-16 code units; a Rust `String` is UTF-8, `len()` counts bytes and `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values.
lessons.rule: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes and `chars().count()` counts Unicode scalar values; neither counts graphemes, and a `String` cannot be indexed by position.

lessons.title: Shared references vs ownership
lessons.concept: Moves instead of shared references
lessons.summary: Assigning an object in JavaScript shares it; assigning a `String` or `Vec` in Rust moves it, and the old binding can no longer be used.
lessons.rule: Each value has one owner: assignment or a by-value parameter moves it, `&T` lends it, and `clone()` makes an independent copy.

lessons.title: Mutating arguments vs borrowing
lessons.concept: Shared and mutable borrows
lessons.summary: A function that changes its argument takes `&mut T`, and one that reads takes `&T`. Many shared borrows or one mutable borrow may exist, never both at once.
lessons.rule: `&T` lends read-only access and `&mut T` lends exclusive write access; neither transfers ownership, and the two never overlap.

lessons.title: TypeScript interfaces vs traits
lessons.concept: Nominal traits instead of structural interfaces
lessons.summary: A TypeScript interface is satisfied by any value with the right shape; a Rust trait is satisfied only by types that explicitly `impl` it.
lessons.rule: A type implements a trait only through an explicit `impl`; use a generic bound for static dispatch over one type and `dyn Trait` for a collection of mixed types.

lessons.title: try/catch vs Result
lessons.concept: Errors as Result values
lessons.summary: `throw` and `try/catch` become `Result<T, E>`: failure is part of the return type, `?` propagates it, and panics are reserved for bugs.
lessons.rule: Return `Result` for a failure the caller can act on, propagate it with `?`, and keep panics such as `unwrap` for bugs and broken invariants.

lessons.title: npm and package.json vs Cargo
lessons.concept: package.json and npm mapped to Cargo
lessons.summary: `package.json` becomes `Cargo.toml`, `package-lock.json` becomes `Cargo.lock`, and npm scripts become built-in Cargo commands, but a bare version number means something different.
lessons.rule: In `Cargo.toml` a bare version such as `"1.3.0"` is a caret requirement, `>=1.3.0, <2.0.0`; pin exactly with `"=1.3.0"`, and let `Cargo.lock` record what was resolved.

lessons.title: Promises vs futures
lessons.concept: Lazy futures and an explicit runtime
lessons.summary: A Promise starts running when it is created; a Rust future does nothing until it is polled, usually by `.await` inside a runtime such as Tokio.
lessons.rule: Futures are lazy: calling an `async fn` only creates a future, and no code inside it runs until something polls it.

lessons/basics/what-is-rust.json.concept: A compiled language without a garbage collector

writing.summary: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector. The compiler checks types, ownership and borrowing before your program runs, then produces a native program.
writing.rule: Rust is a compiled, statically typed language without a garbage collector: rustc checks types, ownership and borrowing before the program runs, then produces a native executable.
writing.explanation:
Rust is a general-purpose programming language for software where speed, predictable memory use and correctness all matter: command-line tools, web servers, embedded devices, WebAssembly modules, and parts of operating systems and browsers. Its first stable version, Rust 1.0, was released in May 2015. A new stable compiler is published every six weeks, and editions such as Rust 2024 let the language evolve without breaking code written for an earlier edition.

Rust is compiled ahead of time. The compiler, `rustc`, reads your source, checks it, and translates it through LLVM into machine code for a target: an iPhone, a Linux server, or `wasm32-wasip1`, the WebAssembly target Crabrix uses to run your programs on the device. The result runs on its own; no interpreter or virtual machine has to be installed. Languages that run source directly, such as Python, or compile it while running, such as JavaScript in V8, discover many mistakes, like calling a method that does not exist, only when the faulty line executes.

Rust is statically typed. Every value has a type the compiler knows, such as `u32`, `String` or `bool`. The compiler often infers types, so you do not write them everywhere, but it never guesses them while the program runs. In the example, `area` promises to take two `u32` values and return one. Passing the text `"3"` instead is error `E0308`, mismatched types, and no program is built, so a program with that mistake never exists.

Rust has no garbage collector, and you do not call `free` either. Each value has one owner, and the value is dropped, its memory released, exactly when that owner goes out of scope. The compiler enforces these ownership and borrowing rules, which is how safe Rust rules out use after free, double frees and data races without a collector running in the background. The rules are introduced gradually in this course and explained in depth in Ownership Mastery.

Two tools do the work. `rustc` compiles a crate; Cargo builds whole projects, runs tests and downloads libraries, called crates, from crates.io. In Crabrix the compiler is part of the app, so Run performs both steps on your device: compile, and only if that succeeds, execute.

recall.question: Rust has no garbage collector. What frees a `String` once your program no longer needs it?
recall.answer: Its owner going out of scope. When the variable that owns the `String` leaves its scope, Rust drops the value and frees its memory exactly once. You never call `free`, and no collector runs in the background.

recall.answer: Rust is compiled ahead of time. `rustc` checks types before it produces an executable; when a check fails it reports an error such as `E0308` and builds nothing, so there is no program to run.

writing.exampleCaption: `?` returns early on the error case, keeping the happy path flat.
writing.explanation:
Pattern matching and the `?` operator keep both cases explicit without null, sentinel values, or exceptions. Reach for `Option` when absence is normal and expected, and `Result` when the caller needs to know why something did not work.

Ask what the caller needs to know when there is no value. If a search simply finds nothing, `Option<T>` describes the two normal outcomes: `Some(item)` or `None`. If a parser fails, `Result<T, E>` describes success plus a reason for failure. Neither type is a disguised boolean. They carry the successful value, and `Result` preserves information needed to explain or recover from the error.

Use `match` when both outcomes deserve visible behavior. `if let Some(item) = lookup()` is compact when you only care about the present case. `map` transforms a value inside `Some` or `Ok` without inventing a value for the other case. `unwrap_or` supplies a deliberate default; use it only when the default is genuinely correct. `?` can return early for an absent `Option` or an error `Result` when the surrounding function has the appropriate return type. A function returning `Result` cannot use `?` on an `Option` without explicitly choosing what error absence means.

For the exercise, make `find(id)` return `Option<Item>` because missing data is expected. Make `parse_id(raw)` return `Result<u32, ParseIntError>` because malformed input has a reason. Combine them in a caller: parse first, then look up, and show distinct messages for malformed and unknown IDs. Avoid `unwrap()` on both paths; it collapses two normal situations into a panic. Good types help the caller write a useful interface.

`Option<T>` answers whether a value is present. `Some(T)` carries the value; `None` means absence. `Result<T, E>` answers whether an operation succeeded. `Ok(T)` carries success; `Err(E)` carries a reason for failure. They are different questions. A search that finds no item may return `None`; a failed file read needs an error that explains what went wrong. Choosing the right type tells callers what decision to make.

Take a lookup function and test three cases: item found, item missing, and storage unavailable. If the last case is possible, a single `Option` cannot communicate it well; consider `Result<Option<T>, E>`. Unwrap only when you have proved the variant or intentionally want to crash on an invariant violation. Prefer `match`, `if let`, or combinators when they keep both paths visible. Ask what information a caller needs at the boundary, then choose the return type.

writing.exampleCaption: The move is what makes a double free impossible.
writing.explanation:
Moves transfer that responsibility to a new binding and make the old one unusable. Copy types duplicate instead of moving, and Drop runs the moment the owner leaves scope — which is how Rust frees memory with no garbage collector and no possibility of a double free. When you genuinely need two usable values, `clone()` makes a second one that owns its own data.

Think of ownership as the answer to one question: who is responsible for cleaning up this value? A `String` owns a growable heap buffer, so there must be a single owner when that buffer is released. In the example, `first` initially owns it. `let second = first` transfers that responsibility; it does not make a second buffer. If both bindings could free the same allocation, the program would be unsound, so the compiler refuses to use `first` afterward.

Trace the example line by line. Before the assignment, `first` is valid. After it, only `second` is valid. At the end of the scope, `second` is dropped and its buffer is freed once. For a small integer, assignment behaves differently because `i32` implements `Copy`: both bindings contain independent bits and remain usable. When you need two independent strings, `.clone()` creates another allocation, and the explicit call shows the cost.

Ownership is also an API design tool. A function taking `String` may keep or transform the value; one taking `&str` only needs to read it. Before adding a clone to silence a move error, ask whether the function should borrow instead. Try passing the example string to a printing function first by value and then by reference. Observe which signature lets the caller print it again. The compiler error identifies where the value moved; use that location to decide who should own the data next.

The same move rule applies when a value enters a collection or is returned from a function. Follow the owner rather than memorizing special cases for each syntax form.

writing.exampleCaption: Nothing happens until the future is awaited or spawned.
writing.explanation:
Calling an `async fn` does nothing on its own: it builds a state machine that makes progress only when polled. `.await` yields at that point, letting the executor run something else while the operation is pending — which is how one thread can service thousands of waits.

Calling an `async fn` creates a future that represents work to be performed. It does not run the body to completion immediately. An executor polls the future; it may return `Poll::Pending`, register a way to be woken, and yield the thread to other tasks. When the awaited operation can make progress, the waker schedules another poll. Eventually the future returns `Poll::Ready(value)`. This is why many I/O waits can share a small number of threads.

An `.await` marks a point where the task may suspend. Local values that are needed afterward become part of the future's state, which affects memory usage and whether the future can be safely sent between executor threads. Code between `await` points still runs synchronously until it yields or completes, so a long CPU loop can monopolize an executor worker even though it sits inside an `async` function.

Write a short `async` function that logs before and after an awaited timer. Observe that constructing its future does not print the whole sequence; running it on an executor does. Then launch two timer futures concurrently and compare the elapsed time with running them one after the other. Avoid thinking of each future as a thread. A future is a state machine plus a polling contract; the runtime decides when and where to poll it. That distinction helps you choose between `async` waiting, blocking work, and true parallel computation.

A future normally needs to be polled by an executor to make progress. Merely storing it in a variable does not schedule it. That is a common source of confusion when an `async` call appears to do nothing. Trace where the future is awaited, spawned, or otherwise polled.

writing.exampleCaption: `created` prints before `fetching`: the future runs only when `block_on` polls it, and the unused one never runs.
writing.explanation:
Calling an async function in JavaScript runs its body synchronously up to the first `await`, and the event loop keeps the rest going. That is why the example prints `fetching` before `created`, and why the unused second call still logs. Calling a Rust `async fn` runs nothing: it returns a value that implements `Future`, a state machine waiting to be polled. Only polling, normally through `.await`, executes the body.

Rust has no built-in event loop. Something must poll the top-level future: an executor such as the Tokio runtime behind `#[tokio::main]`, or, in this example, a ten-line `block_on` that polls in a loop. That `block_on` only suits futures that never wait on I/O; a real runtime parks the thread and uses the `Waker` to resume work when a socket or timer is ready. `.await` itself is only allowed inside `async` functions and blocks (E0728).

Laziness has consequences you can use. A future that is dropped before it completes simply stops, which is how timeouts and `select!` cancel work, whereas a JavaScript promise cannot be cancelled from outside; there is only an `AbortSignal` the callee may honour. Writing `let pending = fetch_price();` and awaiting it later starts nothing early. To run several futures concurrently, combine them with `join!` or spawn them as tasks, the counterparts of `Promise.all` and of starting promises without awaiting them.

rustc helps with the most common mistake. A future that is created and never used triggers the `unused_must_use` warning, unused implementer of `Future` that must be used. Treat that warning as an error in async code; it almost always means a missing `.await`.

Choosing the runtime is part of the program's design.

writing.summary: Every heap value in Rust has exactly one owner; passing it by value moves ownership, and the end of the owner's scope frees it exactly once.
writing.rule: One value has one owner; a move transfers ownership and ends the old binding, and the remaining owners drop in reverse declaration order at the end of their scope.
writing.explanation:
In C, ownership of a `malloc` result is a convention written in comments: who frees it, and when. Getting it wrong has three outcomes: a leak, a use after free or a double free. The example's `archive()` frees its argument and the caller frees it again. Nothing in `void archive(char *)` says the pointer is consumed, so the compiler cannot help; AddressSanitizer reports `attempting double-free`, and a plain macOS build is killed by a trap inside `free`.

Rust makes the convention part of the type. `String`, `Vec<T>` and `Box<T>` own their heap memory. A parameter of type `String` takes ownership: after `archive(report)` the value has moved, and any later use of `report` is error `E0382`, borrow of moved value. The value is freed once, by its final owner, when that owner goes out of scope. There is no `free` to call and none to forget on an early return.

A move copies only the handle (pointer, length and capacity) and then treats the source as uninitialised; nothing is deep-copied unless you call `.clone()`. Returning a value moves it out to the caller, which is how a Rust function hands back ownership, like a C function returning a pointer the caller must free.

Cleanup order is defined. At the end of a scope, the remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order, the order a careful `goto cleanup` chain releases resources. The `Drop` trait runs code at that point, so the same mechanism closes files and releases locks. `drop(x)` ends a value early by moving it into a function that does nothing with it.
writing.exampleCaption: `archive` consumes `report`; the three `Noisy` values drop in reverse order (`file`, `lock`, `log`) after `end of main`.
writing.task: Port the commented C function: `take_largest` returns the longest buffer (the first one on a tie) without copying it, drops all the others, and returns `None` for an empty list.
writing.success: The returned `Vec` has the same heap pointer as the buffer it came from, a tie returns the first longest buffer, and an empty list gives `None`.
writing.question: A function declares `let _log = Noisy("log"); let _lock = Noisy("lock"); let _file = Noisy("file");`. In which order do their `Drop` implementations run at its closing brace?
answers: `log`, `lock`, `file`: declaration order
In an unspecified order, as with a garbage collector
`file`, `lock`, `log`: reverse declaration order
None of them run there: names starting with `_` are dropped immediately
writing.feedback: Remaining locals drop in reverse declaration order. A leading underscore only silences the unused-variable warning; `_log` still owns its value until the scope ends.

recall.question: How does a Rust function return ownership of a heap buffer, the way a C function returns a pointer the caller must free?
recall.answer: It returns the owning type by value, such as `Vec<u8>` or `String`. The return moves the handle to the caller, who becomes the owner and frees it by letting it go out of scope. The heap data is not copied.

recall.question: Does this compile? If not, what is the smallest fix?
recall.answer: No: `data` moved into `consume`, so `data.len()` is error `E0382`. Read the length before the call, or change `consume` to borrow (`v: &[u8]`) and call `consume(&data)`.

depth.correction: There is no collector. The compiler inserts the drop at a known point: the end of the final owner's scope, or the call to `drop`. That point is visible in the source, exactly where a careful C programmer would have called `free`.

writing.summary: Preserve arguments and reject ambiguous input.
writing.rule: Parse the entire invocation before applying any side effect.
writing.explanation:
A shell groups text into arguments before a Rust program sees it. Quotes preserve a space or an empty argument; they are not usually part of the resulting argument. Cargo consumes its options before the double dash and passes the remainder to the executable. The first executable argument is conventionally the program name and is not a user command.

Task Ledger accepts exactly `list` or `add TITLE`. Reject an unknown command, a missing title and extra arguments. Trim the title for domain validation, while retaining internal spaces and Unicode. Do not partially add a task before discovering a later invalid option. The independent lab takes only the already-separated user arguments; the companion main passes `std::env::args().skip(1)`.

The route project is Task Ledger: first keep a reproducible source history, then expose its data through a CLI and HTTP boundary, persist it in SQL, diagnose failures and prepare a release. This lesson owns one contract in that project. Run the worked example before changing the starter and explain which input makes the tempting shortcut fail.

Terminal practice: Run cargo run -- add "learn Rust" and cargo run -- add "" against the companion CLI.

The compiler lab is independent of the reading question. Edit solution.rs; the app supplies a separate caller with normal, empty and adversarial inputs. A successful unchanged demonstration does not prove your implementation. After the lab, apply the same contract to the route companion project. Its README separates the on-device adapter from the desktop Cargo/TCP profile.

Every earlier value has already been checked and is nonnegative. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[1, 2, 3]`, the worked program returns `-1`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[4, 9, -2, 7]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Return the first index whose reading is negative, or -1 when none is negative.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Return the first index whose reading is negative, or -1 when none is negative. On input `[4, 9, -2, 7]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Visit every element once and stop when the predicate is satisfied. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. A scan turns a sequence into a small piece of state. Say what the state means after the first i elements, before you describe a loop body. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n) time · O(1) extra space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Use an empty slice and a one-element slice as checks. Initial values must not silently assume that at least one item exists. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.

# ASCII Histogram

Turn numeric data into a terminal chart.

## What to notice

Each input value becomes a row of repeated characters, turning numbers into a chart you can read in a terminal. Follow the loop that pairs a label with its bar and look at the formatting that keeps rows aligned.

## How it works

The `bar` function repeats one block character for the requested value. `main` keeps day labels and counts together as tuples, then formats each label beside its bar. The display is intentionally proportional to raw counts, so a value of twelve occupies three times the width of a value of four. Change a sample to zero and see how the label remains while its bar disappears. This is a terminal chart, so alignment and character width matter as much as the arithmetic.

## Concepts

- arrays
- repeat
- formatting

## Your challenge

Scale values larger than 20 into a fixed-width bar and label the maximum row.

# Budget Planner

List expenses and calculate a monthly total.

## What to notice

Expenses are records rather than loose strings. Follow one expense from its label and amount into the total and the final report. Changing a single item should change the total by exactly that amount.

## How it works

An `Expense` pairs a label with a floating-point amount. The iterator maps each record to its amount and `sum` produces a monthly total; a second loop prints the individual rows with fixed column widths. There are no categories or persistence in this small example. Add an expense and check that exactly one new row appears and the total changes by that amount. For real money, consider integer minor units or a decimal type instead of binary floating point.
